title: Deploying Next.js (Vercel, Self-Hosting, Static Export)
summary: Shipping a Next.js app means running **next build**, then choosing a target — **Vercel** (zero-config managed), **self-hosting** a Node server (standalone output, often in **Docker**), or a **static export** to any CDN — while handling **env vars in production**, the **edge vs node runtime**, **preview deployments**, and **CDN** caching.

subtopics.title: Building (next build)
subtopics.explanation: `next build` compiles your app for production: it bundles and minifies JS, pre-renders static pages (SSG/ISR), and prints a route summary showing which routes are static (○) vs dynamic (ƒ). You then serve it with `next start` (a Node server). The build output is the contract for whatever you deploy onto, so reading its static/dynamic markers tells you exactly how each route will behave in production.
subtopics.example: next build && next start  // produce + serve the production app

subtopics.title: Vercel deployment
subtopics.explanation: Vercel (the company behind Next.js) offers zero-config deployment: connect a Git repo and every push builds and deploys automatically. It maps Next features to its platform — static/ISR pages to the CDN, Server Components/SSR and route handlers to serverless functions, and edge-runtime code to the edge network. It's the fastest path and supports preview deployments and on-demand revalidation out of the box.
subtopics.example: git push -> Vercel builds, deploys, gives a preview/prod URL

subtopics.title: Self-hosting (Node server / standalone / Docker)
subtopics.explanation: You can host Next anywhere Node runs: `next build && next start`, or use `output: 'standalone'` so the build emits a minimal server bundle with only required node_modules — ideal for small Docker images. In a container you copy the .next/standalone output and run `node server.js`. Self-hosting gives full control (your cloud, your network) at the cost of managing scaling, caching, and ISR storage yourself.

subtopics.title: Static export
subtopics.explanation: `output: 'export'` renders every page to plain HTML/CSS/JS at build time, producing an `out/` folder you can host on ANY static host or CDN (S3, GitHub Pages, Nginx) with no Node server. The trade-off: you lose server-only features — SSR/dynamic rendering, route handlers, ISR, and Image Optimization (unless you supply a custom loader). It's perfect for fully static marketing/doc sites.
subtopics.example: // next.config.js -> output: 'export'; build emits an out/ folder

subtopics.title: Edge vs Node runtime
subtopics.explanation: Next routes can run on the Node.js runtime (full Node APIs, larger cold starts, heavier compute) or the Edge runtime (a lightweight Web-APIs-only environment that runs close to users for low latency, but with limited APIs and no native Node modules). You opt in per route with `export const runtime = 'edge'`. Use edge for light, latency-sensitive/geo logic (middleware, simple handlers) and Node for heavy work or incompatible dependencies.
subtopics.example: export const runtime = 'edge'; // run this route at the edge

subtopics.title: Environment variables in production
subtopics.explanation: Server-only secrets are read via `process.env.MY_SECRET` and stay on the server; only variables prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_` are inlined into the client bundle (so never put secrets there). Crucially, NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are baked in at BUILD time, so changing them requires a rebuild. In production you set vars in your host's dashboard/secrets manager, not in committed .env files.
subtopics.example: process.env.DATABASE_URL // server only; NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL // client, build-time

subtopics.title: Preview deployments
subtopics.explanation: A preview deployment is a full, isolated deploy of a branch/PR at a unique URL, so reviewers and stakeholders can test real behavior before merging to production. Vercel creates these automatically per push; self-hosters replicate them with ephemeral environments in CI. They make QA, design review, and stakeholder sign-off concrete rather than 'works on my machine'.
subtopics.example: PR push -> unique preview URL for review before prod

subtopics.title: CDN
subtopics.explanation: A CDN caches static assets and static/ISR HTML at edge locations near users, so most requests never hit your origin — giving low latency and high scalability. Next's static pages, _next/static assets, and ISR responses are CDN-cacheable; dynamic SSR responses generally aren't (or use short cache headers). On Vercel this is automatic; self-hosting means putting a CDN (CloudFront, Cloudflare) in front of your server.
subtopics.example: CDN serves /_next/static + static/ISR HTML from the edge

foundations.overview: Deploying Next.js starts with `next build` and then choosing where the output runs: a managed platform like Vercel, a self-hosted Node server (often Dockerized via standalone output), or a static export to a CDN. The right target depends on which features you use — SSR/ISR/route handlers need a server, while a purely static site can be exported. Around that you manage env vars, runtime choice, previews, and CDN caching.
foundations.formalDefinition: Deployment is the process of building a production artifact with next build and serving it on a target environment (managed platform, self-hosted Node server, or static CDN host), configured with the correct runtime, environment variables, and caching so each route behaves as designed.
foundations.whyItMatters: How you deploy determines performance (CDN/edge), cost, operational burden, and which Next features are even available. A wrong target — e.g. static-exporting an app that needs ISR — silently breaks features, while the right one gives fast, scalable, low-maintenance hosting.
foundations.mentalModel: Ask: does the app need a server at runtime? If it uses SSR/ISR/route handlers/Image Optimization → deploy with a Node server (Vercel or self-host). If it's fully static → export to a CDN. Then layer env vars, runtime (edge vs node), previews, and CDN caching on top.
foundations.browserPerspective: Users hit a CDN edge first: static/ISR HTML and _next/static assets are served instantly from nearby cache, while dynamic requests fall through to a serverless function or your origin server. Edge-runtime routes execute close to the user for the lowest latency.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A startup pushes to Vercel for zero-config deploys and previews; an enterprise self-hosts via Docker standalone on Kubernetes behind CloudFront; a docs site static-exports to S3/GitHub Pages.
foundations.businessImpact: Managed deploys speed shipping and reduce ops cost for small teams; self-hosting satisfies compliance/control needs; static export is the cheapest to run. Previews accelerate review cycles and reduce production incidents.
foundations.engineeringImpact: The deployment target shapes the architecture — feature availability, caching strategy, and CI/CD. Standalone output and clear runtime choices keep images small and deploys reproducible; misconfigured env vars or runtimes are a common source of prod-only bugs.
foundations.performanceImpact: CDN-served static/ISR content and edge-runtime routes minimize latency; a Node server adds origin compute for dynamic routes. Choosing edge vs node per route and caching aggressively at the CDN are the main production performance levers.
commonUseCases: Zero-config Git-based deploys with previews on Vercel
Self-hosting a Dockerized standalone Node server in your own cloud
Static export of a fully static site to a CDN/object store
Running light, latency-sensitive routes on the edge runtime

commonMisconceptions.myth: Static export ('output: export') works for any Next.js app.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It drops server features — SSR/dynamic rendering, route handlers, ISR, and built-in Image Optimization — so it only fits fully static apps.

commonMisconceptions.myth: NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables can be changed without redeploying.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They are inlined into the client bundle at build time, so changing them requires a rebuild/redeploy.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can only deploy Next.js to Vercel.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Next is a standard Node app; you can self-host with next start or standalone output (Docker, Node, Kubernetes) or static-export to any host.

debuggingLab.title: next build fails after switching to static export
debuggingLab.symptom: After setting output: 'export', the build errors on a route handler and the dashboard, and images stop optimizing.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Static export produces only static files, so it cannot run server features: route handlers, dynamic/SSR rendering, ISR, and default Image Optimization all require a server. The build fails because the app mixes those with output: 'export'. Either remove output: 'export' and deploy to a server target (Vercel/self-host), or remove/replace the server features (drop the route handler, make pages static, and configure a custom image loader or unoptimized images).
commonMistakes: Setting output: 'export' on an app that uses SSR, ISR, or route handlers.
Forgetting that default next/image optimization needs a server or a custom loader.
Assuming export supports on-demand/dynamic data fetching at request time.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Decide the target: if you need server features, drop export and deploy a Node server; if the site is truly static, remove the server features and add a custom image loader (or images.unoptimized).

theory.question: What are the main ways to deploy a Next.js app and how do you choose between them?
theory.directAnswer: After next build you can deploy to Vercel (zero-config, Git-based, maps features to CDN/serverless/edge automatically), self-host a Node server (next start, or output: 'standalone' in Docker for full control), or static-export (output: 'export') to any CDN if the app is fully static. The choice hinges on whether you need a runtime server: SSR/ISR/route handlers/Image Optimization require a server (Vercel or self-host), while a purely static site can be exported.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three deployment targets: managed platform, self-hosted Node server, and static export.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Apps differ in feature needs, control/compliance requirements, and budget, so Next supports several targets.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Vercel maps static/ISR to CDN and dynamic to serverless/edge; self-hosting runs a Node server (standalone for slim Docker images); export emits static files for a CDN.

theory.whyImportant: Picking the wrong target silently disables features or adds needless ops; it's a common production decision and interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: Startup → Vercel; enterprise with compliance → Docker standalone on Kubernetes; docs site → static export to S3.

nestedTopics.explanation: Emits a minimal server bundle with only needed deps for small Docker images.

followUps.question: Can you self-host and still use ISR?
followUps.answer: Yes — next start / standalone supports ISR, but you manage the cache storage and any CDN in front yourself.

theory.question: How do environment variables work in Next.js across build and runtime, and what's the security pitfall?
theory.directAnswer: Variables without a prefix (e.g. process.env.DATABASE_URL) are server-only and read at runtime on the server — safe for secrets. Variables prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ are inlined into the client bundle at BUILD time, so they're public and changing them requires a rebuild. The pitfall is putting a secret in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ var (or referencing a server var in client code), which leaks it into the browser bundle. In production you set vars via the host's secrets manager, not committed .env files.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The split between server-only env vars and build-time-inlined NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Client code needs some config, but secrets must never reach the browser, so the prefix gates exposure.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Build inlines NEXT_PUBLIC_ values into client JS; non-prefixed vars are only available in server code at runtime.

theory.whyImportant: Leaking secrets via NEXT_PUBLIC_ is a real, common security incident.
theory.realWorldExample: NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL is fine in the bundle; STRIPE_SECRET_KEY must stay server-only.

nestedTopics.title: Build-time inlining
nestedTopics.explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are frozen at build, so updates need a redeploy.

followUps.question: Why did changing a NEXT_PUBLIC_ var not take effect in prod?
followUps.answer: It's inlined at build time; you must rebuild and redeploy for the new value to appear in the client bundle.

scenario.question: Your company can't use Vercel (compliance) but the app uses SSR and ISR. How would you deploy it in your own cloud?
scenario.directAnswer: I'd self-host with a Node server. Set output: 'standalone' so next build emits a minimal server bundle, build a small Docker image that copies .next/standalone and runs node server.js, and deploy it (e.g. on Kubernetes or ECS) behind a load balancer. I'd put a CDN (CloudFront/Cloudflare) in front to cache static and ISR responses, configure production env vars via the platform's secrets manager, and ensure persistent storage/shared cache for ISR if running multiple replicas. Health checks and autoscaling handle availability.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A self-hosted deployment of a server-dependent Next app.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Compliance/control needs rule out managed platforms but the app still needs SSR/ISR.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Standalone output + Docker run a Node server; a CDN fronts it for caching; secrets and ISR cache are configured for the cluster.

scenario.whyImportant: Shows you can run Next anywhere, not just Vercel, with correct caching and config.

nestedTopics.title: ISR across replicas
nestedTopics.explanation: Multiple instances need a shared cache so regenerated pages are consistent.

nestedTopics.title: CDN fronting
nestedTopics.explanation: Cache static/ISR at the edge so origin handles mostly dynamic requests.

followUps.question: Why output: 'standalone' instead of plain next start?
followUps.answer: Standalone bundles only the dependencies the server needs, producing a much smaller, self-contained Docker image that's faster to ship and start.

coding.question: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile to self-host a Next.js app using standalone output.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll enable output: 'standalone' in next.config so the build emits a self-contained server. A multi-stage Dockerfile installs deps and builds in a builder stage, then copies only .next/standalone, .next/static, and public into a slim runtime image and runs node server.js. This keeps the final image small and secure.

solution.code:
// next.config.js
module.exports = { output: 'standalone' };

# Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

coding.lineByLine: output: 'standalone' makes the build emit a minimal server. The builder stage installs deps with npm ci and runs next build. The runner stage copies only the standalone server, the static assets (.next/static), and public/, then runs node server.js — no full node_modules, so the image stays small. EXPOSE 3000 and NODE_ENV=production configure the server.
coding.spaceComplexity: N/A — though standalone minimizes image size.

alternativeApproaches.title: Plain next start
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Skip standalone and run next start with full node_modules — simpler but a larger image.

followUps.question: Why copy .next/static and public separately?
followUps.answer: The standalone output doesn't include static assets or the public folder, so they must be copied in for the server to serve them.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Choose a target by feature need: Vercel for managed (CDN + serverless + edge mapped automatically), self-hosted standalone Node (Docker/Kubernetes behind a CDN) for control, or static export to a CDN for fully static sites. Pick edge vs node runtime per route based on latency and API needs.
productionDeepDive.performance: Front the app with a CDN so static/ISR HTML and _next/static assets are served from the edge, leaving the origin to handle dynamic requests. Use the edge runtime for light latency-sensitive routes; keep ISR caches warm and shared across replicas when self-hosting.
productionDeepDive.security: Keep secrets server-only (never NEXT_PUBLIC_); inject production env vars via the host's secrets manager, not committed files. Run containers as non-root, keep base images patched, and avoid leaking server vars into client bundles.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Static/ISR via CDN scales near-free; serverless functions autoscale on Vercel; self-hosted servers scale horizontally with a shared ISR cache and a load balancer. Isolate expensive SSR and cache aggressively to protect the origin.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Use reproducible builds (standalone output, pinned base images), document the deployment target and runtime per route, and rely on preview deployments so every change is verified at a real URL before merge.
productionDeepDive.observability: Monitor build output (static/dynamic markers), CDN cache HIT/MISS, function cold starts and durations, error rates, and Core Web Vitals in production; wire logs/metrics from the host (Vercel analytics or your APM).

caseStudies.problem: Needs SSR/ISR but cannot use a managed PaaS for data-residency reasons.
caseStudies.solution: Self-host standalone output in Docker on Kubernetes behind a CDN with a shared ISR cache and secrets manager.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More operational ownership (scaling, caching, patching) vs full control and compliance.
caseStudies.lessons: Next runs anywhere Node does; standalone + CDN gives Vercel-like performance with self-managed infra.

keyTakeaways: Deployment starts with next build; then choose a target based on whether the app needs a runtime server.
Vercel is zero-config (CDN + serverless + edge); self-hosting runs a Node server (output: 'standalone' for slim Docker images); static export targets any CDN.
Static export ('output: export') drops server features — SSR, ISR, route handlers, and default Image Optimization.
Keep secrets server-only; NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars are public and inlined at build time, so changing them needs a redeploy.
Use edge runtime for light, latency-sensitive routes, put a CDN in front to cache static/ISR, and use preview deployments to verify changes before production.
